slides.0.title: Course Introduction
slides.0.content:
Wine is not just a beverage — it is an art of sensory experience. Wine tasting is the professional skill of systematically analysing the characteristics of a wine through sight, smell, and taste. For Bordeaux enthusiasts, mastering the correct tasting method allows you to appreciate more deeply the stories of terroir, craftsmanship, and time behind each bottle.

This course will guide you through the tasting techniques for Bordeaux wines. We will master the five steps of tasting (Appearance → Swirl → Nose → Palate → Conclusion), learn correct glass-holding posture and service temperature, recognise the typical aroma characteristics of Bordeaux red and white wines, understand professional terms such as body, tannins, acidity, and finish, and learn how to use tasting vocabulary to accurately describe your sensations. This is not only a skills training — it is a key to unlocking the sensory world of wine.

Learning Objectives

👁️ Master Visual Observation Techniques

Learn to assess wine age, variety, and winemaking style from colour, clarity, and viscosity

👃 Learn Olfactory Analysis Methods

Recognise the typical aroma families of Bordeaux red and white wines (fruit, floral, oak, and tertiary)

👅 Understand Palate Structure Elements

Master key indicators including body, tannins, acidity, sweetness, alcohol, and finish

🍷 Establish Optimal Tasting Conditions

Learn glass selection, service temperature, decanting timing, and other techniques that enhance the tasting experience

📝 Use Professional Tasting Vocabulary

Build the language ability to accurately describe wine characteristics and effectively communicate your tasting impressions with others

After completing this course, you will be able to taste Bordeaux wines systematically and describe your sensory experience in professional language. Let us begin the journey of sensory exploration!

slides.2.quiz.question: What is the ideal service temperature for tasting a young Bordeaux red wine?
slides.2.quiz.explanation: The ideal tasting temperature for young Bordeaux red wines is 14–16°C. This temperature highlights the fruit and freshness while preventing excessive warmth from emphasising the alcohol.

slides.7.title: Olfactory Evaluation: Layered Aroma Analysis
slides.7.highlights.0.title: Aroma Layers

slides.7.highlights.1.title: Varietal Character
slides.7.highlights.1.content: Typical aroma expressions of different grape varieties
slides.7.content:
The nose is the heart of tasting. The complex aromatic structure of Bordeaux wine requires a systematic analytical approach to be fully understood and appreciated.

🌺 Aroma Layer Structure

Primary Aromas

Source: The intrinsic character of the grape variety

Cabernet Sauvignon
  • Fruit: Blackcurrant, blackberry, blueberry
  • Herbal: Green pepper, mint, bay leaf
  • Spice: Black pepper, clove
  • Mineral: Pencil shavings, graphite
Merlot
  • Fruit: Plum, cherry, strawberry
  • Sweet: Chocolate, toffee
  • Herbal: Herbs, mint
  • Floral: Violet, rose
Cabernet Franc
  • Fruit: Raspberry, redcurrant
  • Herbal: Green pepper, anise
  • Floral: Violet, lavender
  • Spice: White pepper, vanilla
White Varieties
  • Sauvignon Blanc: Grass, guava, lemon zest
  • Sémillon: Honey, beeswax, white peach
  • Muscadelle: Rose, lychee, musk
Secondary Aromas

Source: Aromas derived from the fermentation process

  • Yeast: Bread, biscuit, yeast
  • Alcoholic fermentation: Cream, butter
  • Malolactic fermentation: Cream, nuts
  • Lees contact: Crème brûlée, brioche
Oak Influence
  • New oak: Vanilla, coconut, cream
  • Toast level: Coffee, caramel, chocolate
  • Wood character: Cedar, sandalwood
  • Spice: Cinnamon, clove, allspice
Tertiary Aromas

Source: Complex aromas that develop through ageing

Bottle-Aged Aromas
  • Animal: Leather, game, musk
  • Earthy: Damp earth, forest floor, mushroom
  • Dried fruit: Raisins, fig, dates
  • Spice development: Tobacco, cigar box, spice
Oxidative Development
  • Nuts: Walnut, hazelnut, almond
  • Honey development: Honey, mead
  • Caramelisation: Caramel, toffee
  • Mineral development: Petroleum, petrol (positive characteristic in small amounts)

👃 Nosing Technique

Nosing Steps
  1. Static nose: Without swirling, assess the first impression
  2. Gentle swirl: Swirl gently to release more aromas
  3. Deep swirl: Swirl more vigorously for maximum aroma intensity
  4. Rest and repeat: Rest between assessments to avoid olfactory fatigue
Nose Position
  • Distance from rim: 1–2 cm from the nose to the rim
  • Depth: You may dip your nose slightly into the bowl
  • Inhalation: Short, deep inhalations — avoid prolonged sniffing
  • Nostrils: Try using each nostril separately to compare perception
Building Aroma Memory
  • Association: Compare to familiar everyday aromas
  • Category memory: Build a memory bank organised by aroma category
  • Intensity assessment: Note the strength of each aroma
  • Persistence: Observe how long each aroma lingers

⚠️ Identifying Aroma Faults

Common Aroma Faults
  • Cork taint (TCA): Musty, damp cardboard
  • Over-oxidation: Sherry-like, vinegary
  • Reduction: Sulphur, rotten egg
  • High volatile acidity: Vinegar, nail polish remover
  • Bacterial contamination: Mousy, putrid
Handling Faults
  • Confirm the judgment: Re-assess several times to confirm a genuine fault
  • Severity assessment: Evaluate the degree of the fault
  • Possible remedy: Determine whether decanting might improve matters
  • Accept or reject: Decide whether to accept the bottle
slides.7.quiz.question: In Bordeaux wines, which grape variety is typically associated with the aroma of "pencil shavings"?
slides.7.quiz.explanation: Pencil shavings or graphite is a typical primary aroma characteristic of Cabernet Sauvignon, especially commonly encountered in quality wines from Bordeaux's Left Bank.

slides.9.highlights.0.title: Process Thinking
slides.9.highlights.0.content: A fixed sequence reduces omissions and produces more consistent evaluations
slides.9.highlights.1.title: Breaking Down Elements
slides.9.highlights.1.content: Note appearance, nose, palate, structure, and conclusion in separate sections
slides.9.content:
Following a fixed tasting sequence helps you record a wine's performance quickly, completely, and consistently.

  1. Appearance: Colour (hue / depth), clarity, viscosity (legs / tears).
  2. Nose:
    • First static impression → gentle swirl → vigorous swirl; avoid olfactory fatigue.
    • Intensity, aroma type (Primary / Secondary / Tertiary), condition (Clean / Faulty).
  3. First sip (Palate): Take a small sip, let the wine coat the palate, briefly draw in air, then swallow or spit.
  4. Palate element analysis:
    • Sweetness | Acidity | Tannins | Alcohol | Body.
    • Flavour intensity and profile — does it align with the nose?
    • Finish: length and texture.
  5. Structure and quality assessment: Balance, Complexity, Concentration.
  6. Maturity and development: Young / Approaching peak / Developing / Mature; ageing potential.
  7. Conclusion: Quality level (e.g. Acceptable / Good / Very Good / Outstanding); suggested drinking window and food pairing.

Tip: Work from the whole to the detail, then return to the whole. Pause 3–5 seconds at each step to allow the brain to recognise and label what it perceives.
slides.10.title: Faults vs. Features: How to Tell the Difference?
slides.10.highlights.0.title: Degree Determines the Verdict
slides.10.highlights.0.content: A trace amount may add complexity; an excess becomes a fault
slides.10.highlights.1.title: Cross-Validation
slides.10.highlights.1.content: Corroborate nose and palate observations to avoid misjudgment from a single impression
slides.10.content:
Many sensations depend on "degree" and "context." The table below helps with quick assessment.

Phenomenon Positive Feature (acceptable / adds value) Negative Fault (unacceptable) Assessment Cue
Slight oxidation Nutty / caramel / honeyed complexity (aged style) Obvious Sherry / vinegar notes; fruit masked Check if colour is too deep; whether palate is flat
Reduction Very faint flint / gunpowder character Rotten egg / rubber / strong sulphur Does swirling improve it? Is it persistent and dominant?
Volatile acidity (VA) Very low levels enhance aromatic lift Pungent vinegar / nail-polish-remover note Strong nasal irritation; disrupts balance
Brettanomyces (barnyard / leather) Very low levels add wildness (acceptable in some styles) Dominant barnyard / ointment / plaster character Does it mask varietal and regional typicity?
TCA (cork taint) — Musty / damp cardboard; flavour compressed Almost no remedy; usually classified as a fault
SO₂ (sulphur dioxide) Reasonable antimicrobial and antioxidant protection Pungent, irritating; suppresses aromas Re-assess after opening and swirling briefly
Sediment / tartrates Natural phenomenon; does not affect quality Hazy / unusual suspended matter Visual check; tartrate crystals settle and are deposited
Bubbles (still wine) A very few may be residual CO₂ from bottling Obvious bubbles and prickling sensation Noticeable bubbles in a still wine are usually abnormal
Oak influence Vanilla / toast / cedar balanced with fruit Wood-dominated; monotone oak overrides fruit Excessive new-oak proportion or heavy toast level

When in doubt: return to the three self-check questions — intensity, balance, and whether typicity is masked.
slides.11.title: Sample Tasting Note: Sentence Templates
slides.11.highlights.0.title: Ready to Use
slides.11.highlights.0.content: Simply swap in the key descriptors to complete a tasting note quickly
slides.11.highlights.1.title: Top-Down Approach
slides.11.highlights.1.content: Structure before flavour; overall impression before detail
slides.11.content:
Appearance

  • "The wine is clear, with a (pale / medium / deep) (ruby / garnet / brick red | lemon / gold) colour; viscosity is (low / medium / high)."
  • "The rim shows (purple / orange / brown) tinges, indicating (youth / development / age)."

Nose

  • "Aroma intensity is (light / medium / pronounced), with (blackcurrant / blackberry / plum…) as primary aromas, accompanied by (vanilla / coconut / toast) as secondary aromas and (leather / tobacco / dried fruit) as tertiary aromas."
  • "Overall condition is clean, with no obvious faults."

Palate

  • "Sweetness: (dry / off-dry / medium-sweet / sweet); acidity: (low / medium / high); tannins: (fine / ripe / grippy) and (low / medium / high); alcohol: (low / medium / high); body: (light / medium / full)."
  • "Flavour intensity: (light / medium / pronounced), dominated by (fruit / spice / oak / tertiary) character; (consistent / inconsistent) with the nose."
  • "Finish: (short / medium / long), with a (clean / bitter / astringent / sweet) texture."

Assessment and Conclusion

  • "Overall balance / complexity / concentration is (acceptable / good / outstanding); quality level judged as (Acceptable / Good / Very Good / Outstanding)."
  • "Maturity: (still young / approachable / approaching peak / mature); potential: (drink now / can age a further X–Y years)."
  • "Food pairing suggestions: (roast beef / lamb / hard cheese / seafood) (one or two examples suffice)."

Practical tip: First jot down key descriptors using the template, then link the sentences into natural prose.

slides.13.title: Lesson Complete
slides.13.description: Congratulations on completing the foundational study of Bordeaux wine tasting and evaluation! You have mastered the complete tasting process (visual, olfactory, and palate), learned to use professional terminology to describe wines, and can identify the classic aromas and flavour characteristics of Bordeaux. These skills will help you understand and enjoy Bordeaux wine more deeply, and share your tasting experiences with others.
